scaladoc-annotation is a single Java jar, with no Scala suffix, for all of them. sbt-scaladoc works with sbt 1.5.8+ and sbt 2.x, and the Gradle plugin with Gradle 8.5+. Scala 2 artifacts target Java 8, Scala 3 ones Java 17 (Scala 3.9 needs it), and run on any later JDK.

docs.title: Where to go next

docs.text:
Talk is cheap. Show me the code. — Linus Torvalds
A module plays one of two parts, sometimes both. It publishes its scaladoc, keeping the doc comments of its classes readable after it’s compiled. Or it reads scaladoc, calling Scaladoc.of or Typedoc.of to get it. In a typical project, a module of models publishes, and the module that derives schemas from them reads.
Each part needs something different, and what that is depends on the Scala version, because Scala 2 and Scala 3 keep doc comments in very different places:
Scala 2 Scala 3 Publishing the compiler plugin, scaladoc-annotation nothing Reading scaladoc-parser scaladoc-parser, -Xread-docs
Scala 2 forgets doc comments once it’s done compiling, so a publishing module needs the compiler plugin, which writes them into the bytecode before they’re lost, in an annotation. The annotation lives in scaladoc-annotation, a jar with one class and no dependencies, and the publishing module depends on it: its classes refer to the annotation, and whatever uses them gets the jar along, the way it gets scala-library. Scala 2 would do without it, but Scala 3 doesn’t compile against such classes when it’s missing, so a Scala 3 project couldn’t use a 2.13 library published this way. Scala 3 keeps doc comments in its TASTy files on its own; a reading module needs -Xread-docs, the option that tells the compiler to load them.
A reading module calls Scaladoc.of or Typedoc.of, so it depends on scaladoc-parser like on any library it calls; scaladoc-core, the model, comes with it. The rest is compiler setup, which is where the sbt and Gradle plugins help: they add the compiler plugin, with scaladoc-annotation, on Scala 2 and -Xread-docs on Scala 3. Maven gets a few lines of POM, and scala-cli a few using directives.
docs.title: Getting started

docs.text:
Add sbt-scaladoc to project/plugins.sbt:
addSbtPlugin("io.github.andyglow" % "sbt-scaladoc" % "0.6.0")
and enable it on the modules whose compiler it should set up: those that publish on Scala 2, and those that read on Scala 3. A module that reads scaladoc adds the parser itself:
lazy val model = project
  .enablePlugins(ScaladocPlugin)            // publishes its scaladoc

lazy val schemas = project
  .dependsOn(model)
  .enablePlugins(ScaladocPlugin)            // on Scala 3, for -Xread-docs; a Scala 2 reader doesn't need it
  .settings(
    // reads it with Scaladoc.of and Typedoc.of; scaladocVersion keeps the parser in step with the plugin
    libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-parser" % scaladocVersion.value
  )
On Scala 2, a module the plugin is enabled on embeds its scaladoc, even one that only reads, as when it’s cross-built for Scala 3 and keeps the plugin for that. It does no harm: a few annotations in its bytecode. A module that shouldn’t embed any doesn’t enable the plugin.
On Scala.js, the parser is the _sjs1 artifact: on sbt 2, %% picks it by itself in a Scala.js module; on sbt 1, use %%%. The compiler plugin runs inside scalac, which is a JVM program however its output is used, so the plugin adds the JVM artifact to Scala.js modules too.
The compiler plugin gets the sbt plugin’s own version, and scaladocVersion overrides it. The other settings tune what the compiler plugin embeds:
Setting Default What it does scaladocVersion plugin’s the version of the compiler plugin scaladocIncludePaths none Scala 2: embed only classes from source files matching these globs scaladocExcludePaths none Scala 2: don’t embed classes from source files matching these globs scaladocIncludeClasses none Scala 2: embed only classes whose name matches these patterns scaladocExcludeClasses none Scala 2: don’t embed classes whose name matches these patterns
The patterns are explained in Choosing what to embed.
docs.title: The sbt plugin

docs.text:
A Scala 2 module that publishes its scaladoc needs the compiler plugin, and the annotation it embeds scaladoc in:
addCompilerPlugin("io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-compiler-plugin" % "0.6.0")
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" % "scaladoc-annotation" % "0.6.0"   // one `%`: a Java jar
A module that reads scaladoc needs the parser, which brings scaladoc-core along:
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-parser" % "0.6.0"
and on Scala 3, -Xread-docs as well:
scalacOptions += "-Xread-docs"
On Scala.js, the parser is the _sjs1 artifact: %% picks it by itself on sbt 2, and sbt 1 needs %%%. The compiler plugin is the JVM artifact, %% on both, and scaladoc-annotation the same Java jar everywhere.
docs.title: By hand
Gradle

docs.text:
Maven builds Scala with scala-maven-plugin, and what a module needs fits into its configuration. The examples below are for Scala 2.13; for 2.12, change the _2.13 suffixes.
A Scala 2 module that publishes its scaladoc needs the compiler plugin, and the annotation it embeds scaladoc in, at the default compile scope, so that it reaches the module’s consumers:
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.andyglow</groupId>
    <artifactId>scaladoc-annotation</artifactId>
    <version>0.6.0</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>net.alchim31.maven</groupId>
      <artifactId>scala-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      <configuration>
        <compilerPlugins>
          <compilerPlugin>
            <groupId>io.github.andyglow</groupId>
            <artifactId>scaladoc-compiler-plugin_2.13</artifactId>
            <version>0.6.0</version>
          </compilerPlugin>
        </compilerPlugins>
        <args>
          <!-- optional: what to leave out, see "Choosing what to embed" -->
          <arg>-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:exclude:class:com.acme.**.internal.*</arg>
        </args>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
The include and exclude patterns are the compiler plugin’s options, one <arg> each; see Choosing what to embed. A Scala 3 module that publishes needs nothing at all.
A module that reads scaladoc needs the parser, which brings scaladoc-core along:
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.andyglow</groupId>
  <artifactId>scaladoc-parser_2.13</artifactId>
  <version>0.6.0</version>
</dependency>
On Scala 3, that’s with the _3 suffix, and -Xread-docs as well:
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>net.alchim31.maven</groupId>
      <artifactId>scala-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      <configuration>
        <args>
          <arg>-Xread-docs</arg>
        </args>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
This setup is tested as a real Maven build, on Scala 2.13, 2.12 and 3, with scala-maven-plugin 4.10 and Maven 3.10: see modules/tests/maven in the repository.
Note The groupId changed in 0.1.0, from com.github.andyglow to io.github.andyglow. Versions up to 0.0.14 stay available under the old one. To upgrade from them, change the groupId along with the version.

docs.text:
The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. — Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
A doc comment looks like prose, but it’s a small language with a grammar of its own. Scaladoc defined most of it: the * border, the @ tags, a wiki markup with ''italic'' and [[links]]. Over the years, comments picked up some HTML and a few habits from javadoc along the way, and real codebases contain all of it, often in the same comment.
The parser reads all of it, and this page walks through what it understands, from the outside in: first the comment as a whole, then its tags, then the markup inside them. That markup is scaladoc’s wiki syntax, Scala 2’s, unless the comment is in Markdown, Scala 3’s default, which the last part is about. Every example on this page is compiled and run when the site is built, so what you see after each snippet is what the parser really returns.
docs.title: Comment syntax
The comment

docs.text:
Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. — Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer
A tag starts a line with @ and its name. Everything up to the next tag is its text, and the text before the first tag is the description. An @ in the middle of a line, as in an e-mail address or @tailrec, is just a character:
Scaladoc.fromString(
  """/** Sends mail to support@example.com, see `@tailrec`.
    |  *
    |  * @param to   who gets it
    |  * @param body what it says,
    |  *             over two lines
    |  * @throws java.io.IOException if the server is down
    |  * @return the message id
    |  */""".stripMargin).map(_.tags.map(_.productPrefix))
// res3: Either[ScaladocException, List[String]] = Right(
//   value = List("Description", "Param", "Param", "Throws", "Returns")
// )
These are the tags the model knows by name. Any other one, like @contentDiagram, comes back as an OtherTag with its name and text.
Tag Model Text the text before the first tag Description markup @constructor Constructor markup @param name Param(name, ...) markup @tparam name TypeParam(name, ...) markup @return (or @returns) Returns markup @throws type Throws(type, ...) markup @see, @note, @example See, Note, Example markup @usecase UseCase markup @todo, @deprecated, @migration Todo, Deprecated, Migration markup @author, @version, @since Author, Version, Since plain text @group id Group(id) none @groupname id GroupName(id, ...) plain text @groupdesc id GroupDescription(id, ...) markup @groupprio id n GroupPriority(id, n) a number @documentable, @inheritdoc Documentable, InheritDoc none anything else OtherTag(name, ...) markup
A tag without text is dropped, since it says nothing, with two exceptions that scaladoc makes as well: @deprecated deprecates even without a reason, and @throws IOException names an exception even without saying when.

docs.text:
I have made this longer than usual because I have not had time to make it shorter. — Blaise Pascal, Lettres provinciales
When a phrase repeats across a comment, @define gives it a name. $name or ${name} then stands for it anywhere in the comment, and \$ is a plain dollar sign:
Scaladoc.fromString(
  """/** Adds an element to the $coll.
    |  *
    |  * @define coll immutable list
    |  * @param x the element to add to the $coll
    |  */""".stripMargin).map(doc => (doc.textDescriptions, doc.textParams))
// res16: Either[ScaladocException, (Seq[String], Map[String, String])] = Right(
//   value = (
//     List("Adds an element to the immutable list."),
//     Map("x" -> "the element to add to the immutable list")
//   )
// )
A define runs up to the next tag, can use other defines, and doesn’t show up in the parsed comment. An unknown variable stays as written.
A comment also uses the defines of its class’s parents and enclosing classes, as scaladoc has it. Only the compiler knows those classes, so that’s Scaladoc.of’s doing: it looks a variable up in the comment itself, then in the base classes in linearization order, and then in the enclosing classes and objects, the same way, outward. The first one found wins, and a define is expanded where it’s used, so a class can change what a parent’s $coll means:
/** A collection of things.
  *
  * @define coll collection
  * @define adds Adds an element to this $coll.
  */
trait Coll

/** A list. $adds
  *
  * @define coll list
  */
class MyList extends Coll  // Scaladoc.of[MyList]: "A list. Adds an element to this list."
The parents’ comments come from where Scaladoc.of finds any comment: TASTy on Scala 3, and on Scala 2 the source when the parent is compiled in the same run, or the scaladoc the compiler plugin embedded in it. On Scala 3, a class’s self type counts when the class is compiled in the same run, since it’s read from the class’s definition. fromString sees a single comment, so only its own defines.
docs.title: Macros
Markdown
What it reads

docs.text:
The parser is checked against the examples of the GitHub Flavored Markdown spec, CommonMark’s plus GitHub’s: 650 of the 672 parse to what the spec expects. The others differ on purpose, the way Scala 3’s scaladoc does, which reads Markdown with flexmark: as a check, the same examples run through flexmark with Scala 3’s options, and the two parse 635 of them alike. The rest are corners where flexmark follows an earlier CommonMark. The parser stays linear on pathological input, like ten thousand unclosed brackets, and nests at most 100 deep, as markdown-it does.
Two things Scala 3 does, the parser doesn’t: :emoji: stays text, since the model has no node for it, and a table’s rows are as wide as its header, missing cells added and extra ones dropped.
docs.title: How it was checked

docs.text:
Scaladoc renders comments to HTML, and this parser turns them into a model for other tools to use. A few choices follow from that difference, and a few from fixing what scaladoc leaves to warnings:
Monospace is literal. Scaladoc parses markup inside backticks; here the text of code stays as written. Unclosed markers are text. Scaladoc runs an unclosed '' to the end of the paragraph. An unclosed <b> or {@code, though, is an error. Bold inside italic works. In ''a '''b''' c'', scaladoc ends the italic at the '''; here the bold nests. Broken tables aren’t tables. Without a valid delimiter row, scaladoc repairs the table and warns; here the lines stay text, which is what GitHub does and what scaladoc’s own source says it should do. HTML becomes the model. Scaladoc passes <b> on as HTML; here it’s Bold, and HTML in code blocks is left alone. {@literal} is text, as in javadoc. Scaladoc shows it as code. $super stays as written. In a class comment, Scala 3’s scaladoc replaces it with the nearest parent’s comment.
docs.title: How this differs from scaladoc

docs.text:
The map is not the territory. — Alfred Korzybski
A parsed comment is a map of the comment, and like every map it leaves things out on purpose. The border is gone, and so are the exact spaces and how a list item was indented. What remains is what the comment says: which tags it has, and how its text is structured. This page is the legend of that map.
docs.title: The model

docs.text:
A Scaladoc is a list of tags, in the order they appear. The description, the text before the first tag, is a tag too. Most tags hold their text as Markup. A few, like @author or @since, hold plain strings, and some, like @documentable, hold nothing. The syntax page has the full list.
Tag      = Description       (Markup)
         | Constructor       (Markup)
         | Param             (String Markup)
         | TypeParam         (String Markup)
         | Returns           (Markup)
         | Throws            (String Markup)
         | See | Note | Example | UseCase | Todo | Deprecated | Migration   (Markup)
         | Author | Version | Since                                       (String)
         | Group             (String)
         | GroupName         (String String)
         | GroupDescription  (String Markup)
         | GroupPriority     (String Int)
         | Documentable
         | InheritDoc
         | OtherTag          (String Markup)

Scaladoc = List Tag
docs.title: Scaladoc and its tags

docs.text:
Markup comes in two kinds: blocks, which stack on top of each other, and spans, which run inline within a block. A Document holds blocks, and a tag’s text is always a Document. The nodes are named for what the markup means, not how it’s written, so '''bold''' in wiki syntax and **bold** in Markdown are both Bold. A few only come from Markdown, since the wiki syntax has no way to write them; they’re marked below.
Span     = PlainText   (String)
         | Monospace   (String)
         | Italic      (List Span)
         | Bold        (List Span)
         | Underline   (List Span)
         | Superscript (List Span)
         | Subscript   (List Span)
         | Strikethrough     (List Span)           -- Markdown
         | Link        (String (List Span))        -- target, title
         | Image       (String String)             -- Markdown: source, alternative text
         | LineBreak                               -- Markdown: a hard line break
         | Checkbox    (Boolean)                   -- Markdown: a task list item's, at its start
         | FootnoteReference (String)              -- Markdown: a footnote's label
         | HtmlTag     (String)                    -- an HTML tag the model has no node for

Markup   = Span
         | Paragraph     (List Span)
         | Heading       (Level (List Span))       -- Level: One to Six
         | CodeBlock     (String (Option String))  -- code, the language a Markdown fence names
         | BlockQuote    (Document)                -- Markdown
         | UnorderedList (List Document)           -- each item: its text and nested lists
         | OrderedList   (List Document Style)     -- Style: Decimal, LowerRoman, UpperRoman, LowerAlpha, UpperAlpha
         | Table         (Row (List Alignment) (List Row))   -- a Row: one Paragraph a cell
         | HorizontalRule
         | Footnote      (String Document)         -- Markdown: label, text
         | Document      (List Markup)
The spans that hold other spans can nest without limit, so walking the model is naturally recursive. Here is a function that collects every link target in a piece of markup, however deep it sits:
def links(m: Markup): List[String] = m match {
  case Link(target, title)     => target :: title.flatMap(links)
  case Document(elements)      => elements.flatMap(links)
  case Paragraph(spans)        => spans.flatMap(links)
  case Heading(_, spans)       => spans.flatMap(links)
  case x: HasSpans             => x.spans.flatMap(links)
  case x: ListBlock            => x.items.flatMap(links)
  case Table(header, _, rows)  => (header :: rows).flatMap(_.cells).flatMap(links)
  case BlockQuote(content)     => links(content)
  case Footnote(_, content)    => links(content)
  case _                       => Nil
}

Scaladoc.fromString(
  """/** See [[scala.Option]].
    |  *
    |  *   - '''also [[scala.Either]]'''
    |  */""".stripMargin).map(_.descriptions.flatMap(links))
// res0: Either[ScaladocException, Seq[String]] = Right(
//   value = List("scala.Option", "scala.Either")
// )
Building markup by hand is just as direct. Every span has a shorthand for the common case of a single piece of text:
Paragraph(PlainText("Use "), Bold("this"), PlainText(" or "), Link("scala.Option"))
// res1: Paragraph = Paragraph(
//   markup = List(
//     PlainText(value = "Use "),
//     Bold(spans = List(PlainText(value = "this"))),
//     PlainText(value = " or "),
//     Link(target = "scala.Option", title = List())
//   )
// )
docs.title: Markup
Text, when markup is too much
Scaladoc.of and Typedoc.of

docs.text:
The Scala 2 compiler keeps a comment only while it compiles the source file the comment is in, and forgets it afterwards. Scaladoc.of therefore checks three places, in this order:
macro attachments, where other macros may have left a comment the @ScaladocCarrier annotation that the compiler plugin adds to the bytecode of a documented class. This is what makes classes from other modules and from jars work the source code, when the class is compiled in the same run as the call
The third place is fragile. An incremental compile that doesn’t recompile the class’s file loses the comment. For anything beyond a single module, the compiler plugin is the reliable way.
docs.title: On Scala 2

docs.text:
Scala 3 keeps doc comments in TASTy, the format it stores type information in, and Scaladoc.of reads them from Symbol.docstring. By default, though, the compiler only loads the comments of the sources it compiles in the current run. To read them from TASTy as well (other modules, jars, and files skipped by an incremental compile), compile the module that calls Scaladoc.of with -Xread-docs (-Yread-docs before Scala 3.5, and deprecated since):
scalacOptions += "-Xread-docs"
The sbt and Gradle plugins add it to every Scala 3 module they’re enabled on, under the name its Scala version takes; Maven builds pass it in scala-maven-plugin’s args.
docs.title: On Scala 3

docs.text:
Scaladoc.of reads a comment in the syntax of where it finds it:
Found in Written for Read as the source code, the annotation (Scala 2) Scala 2 wiki, Scala 2’s only syntax Symbol.docstring (Scala 3) Scala 3 Markdown, Scala 3’s default the annotation, on a Scala 2 class (Scala 3) Scala 2 wiki
On Scala 3, a codebase that writes its comments in wiki syntax, as with scaladoc’s -comment-syntax wiki, says so with a given in scope where it calls Scaladoc.of, or each comment says it for itself, as in Scala 3’s scaladoc:
import scaladoc.syntax.wiki.given   // Scaladoc.of reads wiki from here on

/** Some '''bold''' text.
  *
  * @syntax wiki
  */
Scaladoc.of reads the given’s type, so it’s scaladoc.syntax.wiki or scaladoc.syntax.markdown, which also works in a library that calls Scaladoc.of from its own macros: the given in scope where those expand counts.
docs.title: Which syntax

docs.text: A Scala 3 project can use Scala 2.13 libraries, and their classes have no TASTy to keep doc comments in. When a library was compiled with the compiler plugin, its classes carry their scaladoc in the @ScaladocCarrier annotation, and Scaladoc.of reads it from there, as wiki, the syntax it was written in.
docs.title: Scala 2 libraries on Scala 3

docs.text: A comment whose * border wanders from line to line is usually a sign of a botched edit. Scaladoc.of checks the alignment, on Scala 2 and on Scala 3 alike, and reports a comment it can’t make sense of as a compile error at the call site, with the comment and the reason. A comment without borders is fine; only a border that’s there gets checked.
docs.title: A misaligned comment is a compile error

docs.text:
Typedoc.of[T]’s tree is made of nodes, each with the type’s name and its scaladoc, as Scaladoc.of gives it:
Node For Has Typedoc.Sum a sealed trait or class, a Scala 3 enum its direct children as variants Typedoc.Product a case class, a Scala 3 enum case with parameters its constructor’s parameters as fields, each with its @param Typedoc.Singleton an object, a Scala 3 enum case without parameters Typedoc.Plain anything else
Variants are nodes themselves, so a variant that’s sealed is a nested Sum. Fields have just their name and their @param, not their type’s tree: a tree of fields’ types could loop on a recursive type, and deriving a whole schema is for the code that walks the tree.
Variants come in declaration order, where the compiler knows it: always on Scala 3, and on Scala 2 when the hierarchy is compiled in the same run. A Scala 2 hierarchy from a jar has no order, and its variants come by name, on Scala 2 and Scala 3 alike.
Typedoc.of finds comments where Scaladoc.of does, so on Scala 3 it reads other modules with -Xread-docs, and a Scala 2 hierarchy from another module or a jar needs the compiler plugin. A malformed comment anywhere in the tree is a compile error.
docs.title: Typedoc.of
From a string

docs.text:
The palest ink is better than the best memory. — Chinese proverb
The Scala 2 compiler has a short memory. It reads every doc comment while it compiles a file, then lets go of it, and nothing of the comment reaches the bytecode. A tool that looks at your classes later, from another module or out of a jar, finds the types intact and the prose gone.
The compiler plugin writes the prose down before it’s forgotten. For every documented class and object, it:
validates the comment. One the parser can’t read, like one with a misaligned border, is reported as a warning in the scaladoc category and isn’t embedded. -Xfatal-warnings, or -Wconf:cat=scaladoc:e on 2.13, turns it into an error packs the comment into a @ScaladocCarrier annotation on the class, which stays in the bytecode. For an object, that’s its class, Obj$, and the class of its static forwarders, Obj, when it has no companion class
Scaladoc.of and Typedoc.of find the annotation, so they work for classes and objects from any module or jar compiled with the plugin. The plugin is for Scala 2.12 and 2.13. Scala 3 doesn’t need it, since it keeps comments in TASTy on its own.
The sbt and Gradle plugins add it on Scala 2 modules, and Maven builds list it in scala-maven-plugin’s compilerPlugins. In sbt, by hand:
addCompilerPlugin("io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-compiler-plugin" % "0.6.0")
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" % "scaladoc-annotation" % "0.6.0"
The plugin’s jar has everything it needs to run. The module still depends on scaladoc-annotation, which holds the annotation and nothing else, because its classes refer to the annotation in their Scala signatures. Scala 2 compiles against them without it, and the JVM runs them without it. Scala 3 doesn’t: a Scala 3 module that uses them fails with “Bad symbolic reference … refers to ScaladocCarrier”, even if it never reads any scaladoc. With the dependency at compile scope, the jar reaches every consumer, like scala-library does.
docs.title: Compiler plugin

docs.text:
The annotation is a public, documented format, and this library’s macros are just one way to read it. It’s a plain Java annotation, scaladoc.annotation.ScaladocCarrier, with runtime retention:
Element Holds text() the doc comment as it is in the source tags() whether text() has the comment’s /** and */ markers and * border (true), or is just its content
It lives in a jar of its own, scaladoc-annotation, which has no dependencies and no Scala version suffix. A tool that reads embedded scaladoc its own way, at runtime with reflection or in any JVM language, needs only that jar:
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" % "scaladoc-annotation" % "0.6.0"
ScaladocCarrier carrier = User.class.getAnnotation(ScaladocCarrier.class);
String comment = carrier == null ? null : carrier.text();   // null: no scaladoc was embedded
The text is then yours to process, with this library’s parser (Scaladoc.fromString(text, hasTags = carrier.tags())) or anything else. Tools that read class files directly, without loading them, find the annotation by its name and need no jar at all.
The annotation’s class doesn’t have to be present wherever the annotated classes are used: the JVM loads and runs them without it, and Java reflection then just leaves the annotation out.
docs.title: Reading embedded scaladoc without this library

docs.text:
By default the plugin embeds the scaladoc of every documented class and object. That’s often more than needed, and a comment meant for the team may not be meant for every jar. Include and exclude patterns narrow it down. With sbt-scaladoc they’re settings:
scaladocIncludePaths   := Seq("**/model/**")
scaladocIncludeClasses := Seq("com.acme.api.*")
scaladocExcludePaths   := Seq("**/generated/**")
scaladocExcludeClasses := Seq("com.acme.**.internal.*")
Without it, they’re options of the compiler plugin, and each can be given several times:
scalacOptions ++= Seq(
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:include:path:**/model/**",
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:include:class:com.acme.api.*",
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:exclude:path:**/generated/**",
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:exclude:class:com.acme.**.internal.*"
)
Option Matches include:path:<glob> source files whose path matches the glob exclude:path:<glob> the same, to leave out include:class:<pattern> classes and objects whose fully qualified name matches the pattern exclude:class:<pattern> the same, to leave out
The rules, in the order they’re applied:
Without any include, every class is included. With some, a class is included if its file matches an include:path or its name matches an include:class. An exclude always wins over an include. Path globs use java.nio glob syntax and are matched against the absolute path of the source file, so they usually start with **/. In class patterns, * matches within one segment of the name, ** across segments, and **. zero or more packages: com.acme.**.internal.* matches both com.acme.internal.Secret and com.acme.a.b.internal.Secret. Nested classes are written with dots, as in com.acme.Outer.Inner, and objects are matched by their name, like classes: com.acme.Registry, not com.acme.Registry$. A malformed option fails the compilation, rather than quietly embedding everything.
docs.title: Choosing what to embed

docs.text: No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man. — attributed to Heraclitus
docs.title: Migrating

docs.text:
The sbt and Gradle plugins set up the compiler and nothing else: the compiler plugin on Scala 2, and -Xread-docs on Scala 3 (see below), now on every Scala 3 module they’re enabled on. They no longer add libraries. A module that reads scaladoc depends on scaladoc-parser itself, like on any library it calls; scaladoc-core comes with it: libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-parser" % scaladocVersion.value // sbt implementation("io.github.andyglow:scaladoc-parser_2.13:0.6.0") // Gradle scaladocRead and scaladocEmbed are gone, and so are Gradle’s read and embed. A build that still sets them doesn’t load: scaladocRead := true or read.set(true): replace it with the dependency above. scaladocEmbed := false or embed.set(false): with the libraries gone, a module that doesn’t embed gets nothing from the plugin, so it doesn’t enable the plugin. On Scala 3, where embed never did anything, a module that reads keeps the plugin for -Xread-docs and drops the setting. A module that embeds scaladoc depends on scaladoc-annotation. In 0.5.0 it got just the compiler plugin, which broke its Scala 3 consumers: Scala 3 doesn’t compile against classes that refer to the annotation without its jar, and fails with “Bad symbolic reference … refers to ScaladocCarrier”. The sbt and Gradle plugins now add it on Scala 2; by hand, and in Maven, add it at compile scope: libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" % "scaladoc-annotation" % "0.6.0" Until a library published with 0.5.0 is republished, a Scala 3 project that uses it adds the same dependency itself. Versions before 0.5.0 aren’t affected: there the plugins gave publishers scaladoc-ast, which held the annotation then. An unclosed HTML or javadoc tag is an error. A , , , or another tag the model has a span for, or a {@code, {@link or another javadoc tag, that isn’t closed in its paragraph used to come back as an HtmlTag or as text. It’s now an UnclosedMarkup error, which in Scaladoc.of and the compiler plugin is a compile error that shows how the text goes from the tag: Unclosed : bold claim, never ... Close the tag, or write < for a < that isn’t one. Java-style generics in prose, like Future or List, read as and , so they fail too; List doesn’t, since without href needs no closing. Tags that need no closing, like
, or , are as before, and so are wiki markers without their closers, like x^2. Markup nests at most 64 deep, past which a tag is a MarkupTooDeep error. See Comment syntax. On Scala 3, the libraries need Scala 3.9 and Java 17. They are built with Scala 3.9, the LTS after 3.3, and a project on Scala 3.3 can’t read what a newer Scala compiled, so a Scala 3 project moves to 3.9 or stays on 0.5. Scala 3.9 targets Java 17 and up. On Scala 2 nothing changes: Scala 2.12 and 2.13, and Java 8. The sbt and Gradle plugins pass -Xread-docs on Scala 3, where they passed -Yread-docs. Scala 3.5 renamed the option and deprecates the old name, and Scala 3.3 and 3.4 don’t know the new one, so a module on those still gets -Yread-docs. A build that sets it by hand, like a Maven one, renames it too. The Gradle plugin also counts a scala-library 3.x dependency as Scala 3, which it is from 3.8 on. On Scala 3, Scaladoc.of reads objects from other modules and jars, where it gave None: Scaladoc.of[Guest.type] for a documented object Guest in another module now has its scaladoc, as a class there has. The compiler plugin embeds the scaladoc of objects too, where it embedded only classes’, so Scaladoc.of[Obj.type] reads a documented object from a Scala 2 jar, on Scala 2 and Scala 3. Objects go by the same include and exclude patterns, by their name like classes: a pattern that matches com.acme.Registry now embeds object Registry too, so a build that embeds selectively may want to check what its patterns now cover. Typedoc.of[T] is new: the scaladoc of a sealed hierarchy or an enum, with its variants’, and of a case class with its fields’, as a tree. See Typedoc.of. Scaladoc.of stays as it is. On Scala 3, Scaladoc.of reads doc comments as Markdown, Scala 3’s default syntax, where it read them as wiki before. A codebase that writes its comments in wiki syntax, as with scaladoc’s -comment-syntax wiki, says so with a given in scope at the call site, or a comment with a tag, as in Scala 3’s scaladoc: import scaladoc.syntax.wiki.given // every Scaladoc.of in scope reads wiki /** Some '''bold''' text. * * @syntax wiki */ fromString and fromDocstring take the syntax as a parameter, CommentSyntax.Wiki by default, and honor @syntax too. On Scala 2, Scaladoc.of reads wiki, Scala 2’s only syntax, as before. Scaladoc.of expands the defines of parents and enclosing classes, as scaladoc does, where it left $name as written unless the comment itself defined it. See Macros. And \$ is a $ in every comment, as in scaladoc, where it stayed \$ in a comment without defines. On Scala 3, Scaladoc.of also reads the scaladoc of Scala 2.13 classes, that a library published with the compiler plugin embedded in them, in wiki syntax. It returned None for them before. The model grows the nodes Markdown needs (see The model): Strikethrough, Image, LineBreak, Checkbox and FootnoteReference among the spans, BlockQuote and Footnote among the blocks. Only Markdown comments produce them, so code that walks wiki comments sees nothing new, but a match over Markup that lists every node gets exhaustivity warnings until it handles them. CodeBlock has a language: CodeBlock(value, language), where language is what a Markdown fence names, like scala in ```scala, and None otherwise. Building one is unchanged, CodeBlock("val x = 1") still compiles, but a pattern needs the second field: // 0.5 case CodeBlock(code) => code // 0.6 case CodeBlock(code, _) => code
docs.title: To 0.6

docs.text:
0.5 gives a module only what its part needs. A module that publishes its scaladoc no longer gets the scaladoc libraries along with the compiler plugin, and a module that reads it asks for them.
The sbt and Gradle plugins publish by default, as before, but now add no libraries for that: on Scala 2 just the compiler plugin (0.6 adds scaladoc-annotation back, see above), on Scala 3 nothing. Reading is opt-in. In 0.5.0, a module that calls Scaladoc.of sets (see 0.6 above, which replaces this with a plain dependency):
scaladocRead := true          // sbt
scaladoc { read.set(true) }   // Gradle
Without it, a module that reads gets “not found: value Scaladoc” when compiling, and setting it fixes that. A module that only reads could also turn publishing off, with scaladocEmbed := false or embed.set(false) (gone in 0.6).
By hand, a Scala 2 module that publishes can drop scaladoc-ast (now scaladoc-core) and scaladoc-parser, and keep just the compiler plugin. A Scala 3 module that publishes needs nothing, and -Yread-docs belongs only to modules that read.
scaladoc-ast is now scaladoc-core. It holds Scaladoc itself, the model of tags and markup, and the helpers like textParams and summary, which is more than a syntax tree. Only the artifact’s name changed; the package is scaladoc as before, so no code changes. The plugins add the new name themselves. By hand, rename the dependency:
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-core" % "0.6.0"   // was scaladoc-ast
scaladoc-annotation is a new jar with just the ScaladocCarrier annotation, for anyone who reads embedded scaladoc without this library; see Reading embedded scaladoc without this library. The annotation’s name and package haven’t changed, so classes compiled with earlier versions read as before. scaladoc-parser depends on it on Scala 2, so readers don’t need to add it.
docs.title: To 0.5

docs.text: 0.4 is the release where the parser learned the rest of scaladoc’s syntax: nested markup, link titles, lists, tables, rules, HTML, javadoc’s inline tags and @define. A model that couldn’t hold those had to grow, and code that takes it apart needs a few changes. Code that only builds markup, or only reads text through the text* helpers, mostly doesn’t.
docs.title: To 0.4

docs.text:
Italic, Bold, Underline, Superscript and Subscript held a String. They now hold a List[Span], so markup can nest. Building one from a string still works, through a shorthand on each companion:
Bold("text")                           // still compiles, now Bold(List(PlainText("text")))
Pattern matches on the string need updating:
// 0.3
case Bold(text)        => text
// 0.4
case b @ Bold(spans)   => b.trimmed.plainString     // or walk the spans
Monospace still holds a String: code is taken literally.
docs.title: Spans hold spans

docs.text: Heading(level, text: String) is now Heading(level, spans: List[Span]), so a title can have markup. Heading(One, "Title") and Heading(1, "Title") still build one. A heading’s title is also trimmed now: = Title = gives "Title", not " Title ".
docs.title: Headings hold spans

docs.text: Link(value: String) held whatever was between the brackets, so [[https://x.y Site]] gave Link("https://x.y Site"). It’s now Link(target: String, title: List[Span]), and that link gives Link("https://x.y", List(PlainText("Site"))). Link("scala.Option") still builds one without a title.
docs.title: Links have a target and a title

docs.text:
Code that matches on Markup exhaustively will hear from the compiler about these:
UnorderedList and OrderedList, whose items are Documents Table, with its rows and column alignments HorizontalRule HtmlTag, a span for HTML tags the model has no node for
docs.title: New nodes

docs.text:
The parser now understands more, so some comments that came back as plain text before don’t anymore:
a line like - item is a list item, and | a | b | lines with a delimiter row are a table <b>, <code>, < and the like are markup and characters, not text {@link X} is a link, {@code x} monospace $name is replaced when the comment defines name with @define
docs.title: Text that changed

docs.text:
0.4 also fixes a number of things that 0.3 got wrong. They don’t change the API, but they do change what some comments parse to:
@return is the returns tag, as in scaladoc. @returns still works a tag starts a line, so foo@bar.com is text; and nothing inside {{{ }}} is a tag @throws java.io.IOException keeps its full exception type @deprecated and @throws X are kept without text the * border is optional an unclosed marker, like the ^ of x^2, is text instead of an error that loses the comment one space after the border belongs to the border, and text is always in a Paragraph code blocks lose the indentation all their lines share Tag.Description’s field is markup; the misspelled makrup stays as a deprecated alias
docs.title: Fixes that change results
